Peng, Brucks, Gui et al., Science Advances 12, eaeh8260 (2026) · open access

Digital twins are funhouse mirrors

In September 2026 a team of 23 researchers, led from Columbia Business School, published the largest test to date of whether an AI could use real human survey results as input information to answer new questions as that person would.

The research team ran 19 pre-registered studies covering 164 outcomes on 1,784 participants, each paired with an AI copy — a “digital twin” — built from more than 500 of that person’s earlier answers. The copies proved only modestly better than a generic model: their answers correlated with their humans’ at 0.20 on average, where 0 would mean no relationship and 1 a perfect one. The team documented five systematic ways in which the copies misrepresented the people they were meant to imitate — too uniform, too stereotyped, more accurate for some groups than others, ideologically skewed, and too rational. That conclusion gave the paper its title. They also ran a conventional machine-learning comparison with no language model involved, training a model called XGBoost on other participants’ real answers, to test whether the limit lay in the AI or in the survey data itself.

The research team released everything — data, code, every model answer — publicly, as a testbed for others to build on. This page was built from that release.

Peng, Brucks, Gui et al., Digital twins are funhouse mirrors: five systematic distortions, Science Advances 12(36), eaeh8260, 2 September 2026 · open access

This page walks through the machinery of that study using the real artefacts: the human survey the twins were built from, the prompt the AI received, the answers the twins gave, and the human answers those were scored against. It does not argue a position. It shows what was done.

Digital twin
An AI told to answer as one specific real person, using that person’s own earlier survey answers as its only information about them.
LLM
Large language model — the type of AI behind ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude. Every twin in the study was an LLM given a person’s answers.
Blueprint
The text file of a person’s earlier answers that was handed to the LLM. It came in four sizes, from everything down to nothing.
Prompt
The full set of instructions sent to the LLM in one go: how to behave, the blueprint, and the new question to answer.
Arm
One complete set-up — one LLM, one blueprint size, one set of settings — run across every question. The study published 21 arms; this page adds 8 more.
Temperature (T)
A setting controlling how much randomness the LLM adds when it answers. T=0 means the most predictable answer every time; higher values allow more variation.

How it ran, in five steps

1

2,058 people took a long survey. January to February 2025, three weekly waves, about 500 questions each over roughly two and a half hours.

2

Two weeks later they answered about 80 of those questions again. This shows how consistent people are with themselves — the most anyone could reasonably expect a copy of them to achieve.

3

Each person’s answers were written out as a blueprint and placed inside a prompt, at four levels of detail: everything, a summary, fourteen demographic facts, or nothing at all.

4

Months later, 1,784 of them sat 19 brand-new studies. For every one of their answers, 29 different arms were sent the same question and asked to answer as that person — one request to the AI per question.

5

Every AI answer was placed beside the human one. Across the whole study that is several hundred thousand pairs.

That is far too much to look at, so this page follows one participant through the whole thing: their survey, their blueprint, their 400 follow-up answers, and what all 29 arms said in their place. This person was chosen for having sat 18 of the 19 studies. They are an illustration of how the study worked, not a summary of what it found.

01 — The flow

One survey, two lanes

For every participant, the human lane and the LLM lane begin from the same survey and end at the same new questions, where the two sets of answers are compared. The counts shown are for the one participant this page follows.

The 29 arms

Twenty-one arms are the research team’s published output, unaltered. Eight are Claude arms added by the author of this page, not by the research team; they are marked ours.

Claude (ours)
Haiku 4.5 · full persona T=0 · Haiku 4.5 · summary T=0 · Haiku 4.5 · demographics T=0 · Haiku 4.5 · empty (blank-section) T=0 · Sonnet 5 · full persona default · Sonnet 5 · summary default · Sonnet 5 · demographics default · Sonnet 5 · empty (section-omitted) default

Reading the labels. Full persona / summary / demographics / empty is the blueprint size (see section 4). T is temperature, explained above. + reasoning means the model was asked to think through its answer in writing before giving it. JSON-forced means the output format was strictly constrained. Fine-tuned means the model was additionally trained on this dataset. Centaur is a Llama model that others had trained on psychology experiments. Default means the model was run at its standard settings because it no longer accepts T=0. The two Claude empty arms differ: blank-section showed the model a persona header with nothing beneath it; section-omitted removed the header too.

02 — The survey

The survey everyone took — one person’s answers

Every participant answered roughly 500 questions: demographics, 279 personality statements, cognitive tests, economic preferences, classic behavioural-economics experiments and a pricing exercise. Here is one person’s complete record, written out exactly as it was placed in the prompt.

It appears below as 217 question blocks holding 628 individual answers. Many blocks are grids — one instruction, several statements to rate — and the study’s “500 questions” counts each statement separately. The blueprint keeps the grid structure, so the two counts describe the same thing at different grain.

Search any word to filter. Each block shows the question, its answer options in grey, and this person’s answers marked with a blue rule.

03 — The repeat

The same questions, two weeks later

Two weeks after the third survey wave, everyone was asked about 80 of the survey items again. This gives each person’s agreement with their own earlier answers — a ceiling for how well any copy could match them, since a copy cannot sensibly be more like someone than they are like themselves.

Across the whole panel that agreement came out at 0.817 on the study’s accuracy measure, where 1.0 would be every answer identical and random guessing scores about 0.63. For the participant followed here, 55 of the 80 repeated answers came back the same and 25 changed.

Green in the right-hand column means the answer was repeated exactly; red means it changed. Shift is how many scale points it moved.

04 — The prompt

What the LLM received

The real prompt, with the real strings, assembled exactly as the study’s published configuration files specify. It has five parts, sent to the LLM as one message. Four of them were identical for every arm. Only the blueprint changed — and the four tabs on it show the four sizes.

The new question shown is one of this participant’s 400 — a fabricated headline from the misinformation study — exactly as the human saw it.

1 · System instruction
identical in all arms
You are an AI assistant. Your task is to answer the 'New Survey Question' as if you are the person described in the 'Persona Profile' (which consists of their past survey responses). Remain consistent with the persona's previous answers and stated traits. Simulate their responses to new questions while accounting for human cognitive limitations, uncertainty, and biases. Follow all instructions provided for the new question carefully regarding the format of your answer.
2 · Persona header
identical in all arms
## Persona Profile (This individual's past survey responses):
3 · The blueprint
the only part that varies
4 · Separator
identical in all arms
## New Survey Question & Instructions (Please respond as the persona described above):
5 · The new question
as the human received it

What came back

The LLM answered in words — one of the options listed in the question. The survey’s own codebook then converted that wording to the number the analysis uses, the same conversion applied to the human answers. For the question above, this is what the GPT-4.1 full-persona arm returned:

LLM returned codebook converts it Analysis received

One request per question, one answer back, in the required format. In the arms behind the study’s headline figures the model was not asked to explain or reason first; a few published variants, marked + reasoning in the roster, were.

05 — The follow-up studies

Every arm’s answer beside the human one

Nineteen brand-new pre-registered studies, run months after the survey, on questions and materials nobody had seen before. 1,784 people took part. For each human answer, 29 arms answered the same question in that person’s place. The participant followed here covers 400 questions across 18 of the 19 studies.

The questions come in three kinds. 278 categorical — multiple choice or a rating scale — where an arm matches if it chose the same option. 64 numeric — 0–100 sliders and point allocations — where it matches if within five points. 58 free text, which are shown for reading but not compared.

Each row is one question with the human answer highlighted. The ticks beneath are the 29 arms, grouped and labelled by model family in the order of the roster above. Expand a row to see every arm’s actual answer and the number it was converted to.
